content.text: {"predictors": [{"name": "Supplier Concentration Fragility", "construction": "From 10-K disclosures under SFAS 131 segment reporting, identify firms that disclose material customer or supplier concentration (e.g., any single customer accounting for >10% of revenue). Construct a fragility score equal to the fraction of revenue attributable to the top-3 named customers, averaged over the two most recent fiscal years. Sort stocks cross-sectionally by this score.", "rationale": "Firms dependent on a few large customers bear concentrated demand risk that is slow to be priced; investors underreact to the fundamental fragility, so these firms should command a risk premium.", "higher_returns_for": "high supplier/customer concentration"}, {"name": "Working Capital Acceleration", "construction": "Compute the second difference (acceleration) of non-cash net working capital scaled by average total assets: [(WC_t - WC_{t-1}) - (WC_{t-1} - WC_{t-2})]/avg(TA), where WC = (current assets - cash) - (current liabilities - short-term debt), using annual Compustat data.", "rationale": "Accelerating working capital investment signals aggressive but low-quality growth and future accrual reversals, which the market fails to fully anticipate.", "higher_returns_for": "low (most negative) working capital acceleration"}, {"name": "Order Backlog Momentum", "construction": "Using Compustat item for order backlog (data item ob), compute year-over-year growth in order backlog scaled by sales. Rank firms cross-sectionally within reporting industries; only include firms that report backlog.", "rationale": "Growth in order backlog is a leading indicator of future revenue that is disclosed but under-followed by investors, generating a delayed price response.", "higher_returns_for": "high order backlog growth"}, {"name": "Dividend Initiation Persistence Gap", "construction": "For firms paying dividends, compute the ratio of trailing-12-month common dividends to trailing free cash flow (operating cash flow minus capex). Flag firms whose dividend payout exceeds free cash flow (ratio > 1) for two consecutive years. Sort into unsustainable-payout vs sustainable-payout groups.", "rationale": "Firms paying dividends they cannot fund from free cash flow face future cuts and financing pressure; the market prices the current yield but underprices the sustainability risk.", "higher_returns_for": "low payout ratio (sustainable dividends)"}, {"name": "Intangible Intensity Adjusted Value", "construction": "Capitalize R&D and a fraction (say 30%) of SG&A as intangible capital using perpetual inventory with 20% and 20% depreciation, add to book equity, and recompute book-to-market. Rank firms by this intangible-adjusted book-to-market cross-sectionally.", "rationale": "Standard book value understates the capital of R&D- and brand-intensive firms; adjusting book equity recovers a cleaner value signal that predicts returns better than raw book-to-market.", "higher_returns_for": "high intangible-adjusted book-to-market"}, {"name": "Analyst Coverage Deceleration", "construction": "Using I/B/E/S, compute the change in the number of analysts issuing FY1 estimates over the trailing 12 months, scaled by prior coverage. Focus on the sign and magnitude of coverage decline.", "rationale": "Declining analyst coverage reduces information production and increases neglect, so these stocks become more mispriced and require higher expected returns as compensation.", "higher_returns_for": "large decline in analyst coverage"}, {"name": "Seasonal Earnings Surprise Repeat", "construction": "For each firm-quarter, compute standardized unexpected earnings (SUE) using a seasonal random walk. Construct a signal equal to the average SUE in the same fiscal quarter over the prior three years. Sort stocks by this same-quarter historical SUE ahead of the current quarter's announcement.", "rationale": "Some firms have persistent same-calendar-quarter earnings strength (e.g., seasonal business) that recurs and is underappreciated, leading to predictable positive surprises.", "higher_returns_for": "high same-quarter historical SUE"}, {"name": "Asset Growth Composition Divergence", "construction": "Decompose total asset growth into operating-asset growth (PP&E + inventory + receivables) versus financial-asset growth (cash + short-term investments). Compute the spread: operating-asset growth minus financial-asset growth, scaled by lagged total assets.", "rationale": "Firms whose growth is concentrated in operating (hard-to-reverse) assets tend to overinvest and underperform, while cash accumulation is less prone to overinvestment; the composition refines the asset-growth anomaly.", "higher_returns_for": "low operating-minus-financial asset growth spread"}, {"name": "Volume-Weighted Price Impact Sensitivity", "construction": "Using daily CRSP data, estimate Amihud-style price impact but weight the daily |return|/dollar-volume ratio by the deviation of that day's volume from its 60-day average, averaged over 12 months. This isolates illiquidity that manifests specifically on high-volume days.", "rationale": "Stocks that show large price moves precisely when trading volume spikes are more exposed to fragile liquidity and forced-trading risk, commanding an illiquidity premium beyond standard Amihud.", "higher_returns_for": "high volume-weighted price impact"}, {"name": "Capital Expenditure Timing Reversal", "construction": "Compute the ratio of current-year capex to the average capex over the prior three years, then take the negative of its two-year change so that firms sharply cutting capex after a prior expansion score high. Scale all capex by lagged net PP&E.", "rationale": "Firms retrenching capex after an investment boom are entering a harvesting phase with rising free cash flow and reduced overinvestment, which the market is slow to reward.", "higher_returns_for": "high capex retrenchment score (firms cutting capex after prior expansion)"}]}
